stories.title: AMD unveils CPU-only Helion rack to support agentic AI workloads
stories.summary: Chip designer working with ecosystem partners ahead of planned November launch date
stories.why_it_matters: A credible CPU-only rack challenges the assumption that every AI workload needs GPUs, which could reshape procurement economics for inference-heavy deployments. If ecosystem partners coalesce around Helion, AMD gains a differentiated wedge in the AI infrastructure market where Nvidia currently dominates, potentially easing supply pressure and opening new colocation configurations.
stories.title_zh: AMD发布仅CPU的Helion机架以支持agentic AI工作负载
stories.content:
AMD has unveiled Helion, a CPU-only rack designed to support agentic AI workloads.

Announced by AMD at the OCP Global Summit in San Jose today (October 12), the company said Helion builds on the “open-platform approach” of its Helios rackscale solution, which was launched earlier this year.

Designed for hyperscale customers, Helion is powered by 6th Gen AMD Epyc 'Venice' server CPUs, supporting up to 32,768 CPU cores. However, AMD said users can customize the rack’s configurations by integrating CPU and AMD Instinct GPU nodes in order to match agent execution, model inference, and tailor compute to each deployment’s performance, power, and cost needs.

Available in both liquid and air-cooled versions, AMD says this approach allows users to “create virtually any configuration needed” to support their requirements.

“Agentic AI is not a single workload. It spans personal agents, enterprise applications, code execution and complex workflows, each with different compute requirements,” said Dan McNamara, SVP and GM, compute and enterprise AI, AMD. “To do that takes optimized compute and infrastructure that can adapt to different workloads. With AMD Helion, we are bringing AMD Epyc performance, open software and flexible rack designs together so our partners can build systems around customer needs and make efficient use of available power.”

AMD said it plans to contribute its Helion specification to OCP, making it available to the community for further development and adoption. At present, the Helion agentic rack configurations are still under development with ecosystem partners, but AMD expects them to be available in November 2026

Ecosystem partners working with AMD for Helion’s launch include Cisco, Dell, Hon Hai Technology (aka Foxconn), HPE, Lenovo, Supermicro, and Wiwynn.
stories.why_zh: 一款可信的纯CPU机架挑战了每个AI工作负载都需要GPU的假设，这可能重塑面向推理密集型部署的采购经济性。如果生态合作伙伴围绕Helion形成合力，AMD将在目前由Nvidia主导的AI基础设施市场中获得一个差异化的切入点，有望缓解供应压力，并开辟新的colocation配置方案。
stories.summary_zh: 芯片设计商正与生态合作伙伴协作，为计划于11月发布做准备

stories.title: MN Holdings bags RM294 mil job to build power facilities for a data centre
stories.summary: MN Holdings has won a RM293.88 million contract to construct two high-voltage power facilities serving a data center development in central Peninsular Malaysia. The award highlights the growing order books of Malaysian electrical infrastructure contractors as the country's data center pipeline drives demand for grid connections and substations.
stories.why_it_matters: Power infrastructure contracts of this size confirm that Malaysia's data center boom is translating into real construction activity, not just announcements. Listed utility contractors are emerging as a proxy play on the sector, and the award signals continued developer confidence in securing grid capacity in the central region.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: MN Holdings赢得2.94亿令吉合同，为一座数据中心建设电力设施
stories.summary_zh: MN Holdings 赢得一份价值 2.9388 亿林吉特的合同，为马来半岛中部的一个 data center 项目建设两座高压电力设施。该合同凸显了马来西亚电气基础设施承包商订单的增长——随着该国 data center 项目管线推进，电网接入和变电站需求持续攀升。
stories.why_zh: 如此规模的电力基础设施合同证实，马来西亚的 data center 热潮正转化为实实在在的建设活动，而非仅停留在公告层面。上市电力工程承包商正成为该行业的间接投资标的，此次中标也显示开发商对中部地区电网容量获取的信心不减。
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 12): MN Holdings Bhd (KL:MNHLDG) has secured a RM293.88 million contract to build two high-voltage power facilities for a data centre development in the central region of Peninsular Malaysia.

In a bourse filing on Monday, the infrastructure utilities construction and engineering group said its wholly-owned MN Power Transmission Sdn Bhd had accepted a letter of award (LOA) from an undisclosed Malaysian company involved in providing infrastructure for hosting, data processing and related services.

The exact location of the project was also not disclosed.

The contract involves the construction of two 275-kilovolt (kV) consumer landing stations.

Under the contract, MN Power Transmission will undertake the construction, supply, installation, testing and commissioning of the facilities, including main buildings and related external works.

Construction began in September 2026 and is expected to be completed by August 2027.

MN Holdings executive director Datuk Dang Siong Diang said the contract reflected continued demand for high-voltage power infrastructure to support large-scale data centre developments in Malaysia.

"Our experience in delivering high-voltage substations and power infrastructure positions us well to participate in this growing segment, and we remain focused on executing these projects effectively while continuing to pursue opportunities across the power infrastructure, data centre and utilities sectors across Peninsular Malaysia," he said in a statement.

As at end-June 2026, MN Holdings had an outstanding order book of RM1.64 billion, with projects across the power, renewable energy, data centre and water infrastructure segments.

The group recently closed its financial year ended June 30, 2026 with a near doubling of annual profit to a record RM92.14 million, as revenue jumped 60.8% to RM869.19 million.

This comes as it reported a 98.8% surge in its fourth-quarter net profit to RM23.98 million from RM12.06 million a year earlier, driven by stronger contributions from its substation engineering segment and a reversal of impairment losses.

Quarterly revenue rose 17.9% to RM211.47 million from RM179.42 million, with the substation engineering segment recording a 24% increase in contribution on higher work progress and project activities.

MN Holdings shares rose three sen or 0.76% to close at RM3.96 on Monday, valuing the group at RM2.74 billion. The counted has gained more than 135% year to date.

stories.title: Three Ps of the apocalypse doomed the Firmus IPO
stories.summary: For the best part of a year, Luxury Escapes chief executive Adam Schwab has impersonated the oracle at Delphi on our podcast, incanting his prophecy of Firmus initial public offering doom. I hate…
stories.content:
For the best part of a year, Luxury Escapes chief executive Adam Schwab has impersonated the oracle at Delphi on our podcast, incanting his prophecy of Firmus initial public offering doom. I hate when he’s right, and we’ve since read plenty of salacious dives into the anatomy of this flop.

Therefore, I wasn’t shocked by the outcome and, indeed, I had been somewhat convinced it would fail even before launch. The more interesting question now is whether Firmus can execute a second effort and overcome the main causes of this mess. I call them the three Ps of the apocalypse: the people, proposition and process.

stories.title: Masteel announces 51% stake buy in power infra firm and private placement to raise working capital funds
stories.summary: Steel manufacturer Malaysia Steel Works (KL) Bhd (KL:MASTEEL) on Monday announced the acquisition of a 51% stake in a high-voltage electrical engineering firm for RM12 million to expand into power infrastructure and data centre construction, as well as a proposed placement of nearly 4% of its issued share base to raise up to RM5.78 million for working capital.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Masteel宣布收购一家电力基础设施公司51%股权，并通过私募配售筹集营运资金，以拓展数据中心建设业务
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 12): Steel manufacturer Malaysia Steel Works (KL) Bhd (KL:MASTEEL) on Monday announced the acquisition of a 51% stake in a high-voltage electrical engineering firm for RM12 million to expand into power infrastructure and data centre construction, as well as a proposed placement of nearly 4% of its issued share base to raise up to RM5.78 million for working capital.

The group said in a bourse filing that the acquisition of Anpec Global Corporation Sdn Bhd will allow it to tap into the latter's engineering capabilities and contracts with major utility companies, including Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA) and Sabah Electricity Sdn Bhd.

Masteel has entered into a share sale agreement with Anpec founder and CEO Abd Rasid Mohamed Salleh for the acquisition. The purchase will be satisfied through RM3 million cash from internal funds, and the issuance of 45 million new Masteel shares at 20 sen apiece — a 7.93% premium to Masteel's five-day volume-weighted average market price (VWAMP) of 18.53 sen up to Oct 9.

This means Abd Rasid, who will retain a 49% interest in Anpec and continue overseeing its operations, will emerge as a substantial shareholder of Masteel with a 5.7% stake. This will be eventually diluted to 5.49% upon completion of the subsequent share placement.

Anpec specialises in high-voltage electrical infrastructure, substations and industrial electrical systems. It has an outstanding order book of RM107 million from six ongoing projects, with completion dates extending to 2028. It has also ventured into data centre-related power infrastructure, having completed a 275kV bulk electricity supply project for the Marmot Data Centre in Elmina West, Selangor, in December 2025.

The company is now bidding for roughly RM63 million worth of jobs involving TNB substations and high-voltage equipment testing services for Sabah Electricity.

Masteel executive vice-chairman Datuk Seri Tai Hean Leng said the acquisition would allow the group to combine its steel manufacturing operations with Anpec's expertise in power infrastructure engineering. The group is aiming to pursue opportunities arising from TNB's RM15 billion investment in the national electricity grid infrastructure, as highlighted under Budget 2027.

"We are positioned to execute larger green energy transition projects, providing green-certified steel alongside 132kV and 275kV substation engineering to connect large-scale solar facilities to the grid," he said in a statement.

The acquisition is targeted for completion by the end of 2026.

The subsequent share placement involves up to 29.48 million new shares, or 3.96% of its issued share base, to investors to be identified at an indicative price of 19.6 sen per share. The final price will be capped at a maximum discount of 10% to the five-day VMAMP before the price-fixing date.

Of the proceeds, RM5.53 million will be used for working capital, including utilities, staff costs and administrative expenses. The balance will be used to defray the proposal's expenses.

Together with the 45 million consideration shares to be issued for the Anpec acquisition, the group will be issuing up to 74.48 million new Masteel shares, equivalent to 10% of its existing issued share capital.

The group previously completed a private placement in August 2025, raising RM13.82 million from issuing 67.5 million new shares. Proceeds from that have since been fully utilised for working capital and related expenses.

Shares of Masteel, which manufactures steel billets, high-tensile deformed steel bars and mild steel round bars, rose 0.5 sen or 2.7% to close at 19 sen on Monday, valuing the company at RM141.9 million.

stories.title: Bipartisan AI inquiry urges Labor to invest in data centres
stories.summary: A bipartisan parliamentary inquiry in Australia has recommended that the Labor government increase investment in data center infrastructure to support the country's artificial intelligence ambitions. The report frames domestic computing capacity as strategically essential, urging policy support to keep AI workloads and associated economic activity onshore.
stories.why_it_matters: Bipartisan backing removes much of the political risk around government support for data centers, opening the door to incentives, streamlined approvals, or direct funding in Australia. Operators and investors can now plan around a friendlier policy environment, though energy grid impacts will draw countervailing pressure.
stories.title_zh: 澳大利亚两党AI调查敦促工党政府投资数据中心
stories.summary_zh: 澳大利亚一项两党联合议会调查建议工党（Labor）政府加大对 data center 基础设施的投资，以支撑该国的人工智能发展雄心。报告将本土算力定位为具有战略必要性的资产，敦促政府出台政策支持，把 AI 工作负载及相关经济活动留在国内。
stories.why_zh: 两党共同支持在很大程度上消除了政府扶持 data center 的政治风险，为澳大利亚出台激励措施、简化审批或直接投资打开了大门。运营商和投资者可以围绕更友好的政策环境制定规划，但电网承载压力也将引来反向的制约声音。
stories.content:
A bipartisan parliamentary inquiry into artificial intelligence has taken the unprecedented step of writing to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, urging the government to invest in data centres in the national interest and insisting that independent assessors have high-level access to model developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic to monitor their activities in real time.

The committee has also given the Albanese government approval to press ahead with changes to copyright laws that will make it easier for major AI developers to train their models in local data centres.

stories.title: Number of data center fires and power failures has doubled since 2024
stories.summary: New data from the Energy Incident Register reveals increasing faults
stories.title_zh: 自2024年以来数据中心火灾和电力故障数量翻倍
stories.content:
Data center fires and power failures have more than doubled since 2024, new incident data has revealed.

According to the Energy Incident Register, which provides an independently run public register of safety incidents in energy and grid infrastructure, the number of fires or power failures at data centers rose from just eight in 2024 to 20 in 2025 and 19 in 2026.

The Energy Incident Register now tracks data center incidents, based on public reporting, from 2010 to 2026 across 26 countries. Of 93 data center incidents in the period, 47 occurred in 2024 or later.

The US suffered the most from these incidents, with 33 incidents across the 16 year period – though this is to be expected given its market share. The UK saw the next highest incidence rate, with 14 incidents across the period.

Some 52 of the 93 incidents were fires or thermal events, with 18 classified as major.

The most common failures were in Uninterruptible Power Systems (UPS) and battery rooms, which represent 22 of the 93 incidents. Backup generators came next, with 15 incidents.

However, in the majority of incidents (53 of 93), no part was named in reporting.

*DCD* has reported on several major incidents at data centers this year, the latest being a fire at a data center in Gasan-dong, Seoul, South Korea, in September, and a fire in a Tata Communications center in India in June.
stories.summary_zh: Energy Incident Register 的新数据显示故障日益增多

stories.title: The huge lurking leverage of AI hyperscalers
stories.summary: While equity investors look to sunny futures, creditors are scrutinising liabilities like data centre leases

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
While equity investors look to sunny futures, creditors are scrutinising liabilities like data centre leases

AT TIMES, creditors can feel like they are the only adults in the room. As artificial intelligence-driven exuberance drives stock markets higher, bond vigilantes are pushing Treasury rates higher, while credit markets are repricing data centre-related debt lower.

While equity analysts might get paid for dreamy earnings forecasts, the best creditors can hope for is repayment at par if a bond is held to maturity.

So they look at the details where, as ever, devils reside. For example, while the debt being taken on by hyperscalers to build out AI infrastructure is getting lots of attention and is even being blamed for crowding out Treasury bonds, creditors have taken this a step further in typically geeky fashion, scrutinising off-balance-sheet obligations such as leases.
stories.summary_zh: 当股票投资者展望未来一片光明时，债权人正在审视诸如数据中心租约之类的负债

stories.title: Tencent tells investors its US$5 bil bond mainly for AI capex
stories.summary: Tencent Holdings told fixed-income investors that its planned bond offering of roughly US$5 billion will primarily fund AI-related capital expenditures, according to people familiar with the matter. The disclosure signals the Chinese internet giant is accelerating spending on AI infrastructure as it competes in the domestic race for computing capacity.
stories.why_it_matters: One of China's largest tech firms explicitly tapping bond markets for AI capex marks a shift in how the country's AI buildout is financed. It signals sustained GPU and data center demand in China despite chip export restrictions, and gives creditors a clearer line of sight into how aggressively Chinese hyperscalers plan to spend.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Tencent向投资者表示，其50亿美元债券主要用于AI资本支出
stories.summary_zh: 据知情人士透露，腾讯控股向固定收益投资者表示，其计划发行的约 50 亿美元债券将主要用于 AI 相关的资本支出。这一披露表明，这家中国互联网巨头正加快 AI 基础设施投入，以在国内算力竞争中占据有利位置。
stories.why_zh: 中国最大科技公司之一明确通过债券市场为 AI 资本支出融资，标志着中国 AI 建设融资方式的转变。这表明即便在芯片出口管制之下，中国对 GPU 和 data center 的需求仍将持续，也让债权人更清楚地看到中国 hyperscaler 的投入力度。
stories.content:
(Oct 12): Tencent Holdings Ltd told fixed-income investors Monday that its planned bond offering of about US$5 billion (RM20.4 billion) will help finance AI-related capital expenditures, people familiar with the matter said, as it doubles down on the sector.

The Chinese technology and gaming giant could price the deal as early as Tuesday, it said in a call with the investors, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. The offering includes US$1.5 billion to US$2 billion across dollar tranches, and 20 billion yuan to 25 billion yuan from offshore yuan notes, the people said.

The proceeds will be primarily for general corporate purposes, such as AI-related capital expenditure, with the bulk of such spending directed toward chip purchases, the people added, citing Tencent’s management.

Both global and Chinese tech companies are increasingly turning to capital markets to fund costly AI investments, even as investors start to scrutinise whether spending on data centres, chips and model development will generate adequate returns.

SoftBank Group Corp recently raised US$11.1 billion through one of the largest corporate junk-bond offerings on record, while Alibaba Group Holding Ltd scooped up a record US$10.2 billion via a follow-on offering. Chinese AI model maker Z.AI Co garnered US$9.6 billion through its IPO, placements and convertible bonds.

Tencent said in the investor call that it currently has no plans to issue shares or convertible bonds, added the people, citing the company.

Tencent didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Tencent is also ramping up its AI-related spending amid a push to catch up to rivals such as ByteDance Ltd and Alibaba. The company hiked capital expenditures by 176% on AI projects and computing to 52.8 billion yuan in the June quarter, triggering a free-cash outflow of 13.8 billion yuan.

Tencent’s capital expenditure is likely to remain elevated through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027, suggesting annual spending of slightly more than 200 billion yuan based on second-quarter levels, the people said.

stories.title: Sponsored: Making every watt work
stories.summary: nVent’s David Wood explores how real-time power intelligence could be the key to unlocking stranded data center capacity and securing responsive AI infrastructure
stories.content:
Across the data center industry, the race to support AI is increasingly being measured in megawatts. As workloads become more demanding and compute densities continue to rise, operators are having to think carefully about how power is delivered and, crucially, how effectively it can be used.

While the conversation often starts at the facility level, the real challenge begins much closer to the rack.

For nVent, the rack itself is becoming a critical point of control. As AI workloads introduce rapid fluctuations in power demand, the ability to monitor and respond in real time will increasingly determine how effectively secured capacity can be utilized.

“The ceiling isn’t really about the silicon,” says David Wood, senior product manager of smart power at nVent. “It’s about power, and specifically, how intelligently you can deliver it.”

With more than 20 years of experience in the data center industry, Wood has witnessed the evolution of power infrastructure first-hand. Now, in a recent DCD>Broadcast episode, he shares why the next step will be about giving the rack the intelligence to respond to increasingly dynamic workloads.

## The rack-level power problem

Data center capacity is often discussed in terms of the overall power available to a facility. Operators may have 20, 50 or even more than 100MW at their disposal, but this doesn’t necessarily mean all this capacity can be put to work. As Wood explains:

“The constraint almost never shows up at this scale. It’s evident inside a single rack.”

At the rack level, provisioned power is either converted into useful compute or becomes stranded because something further downstream can’t respond quickly enough to the demands placed upon it.

Traditional enterprise workloads were relatively predictable, allowing infrastructure to be designed around stable patterns of consumption. AI workloads are an entirely different beast.

GPU clusters can rapidly move between idle and full power draw as workloads shift between training, inference, and communication cycles. Crucially, these changes can happen within milliseconds, creating a level of volatility that conventional infrastructure wasn’t designed to manage.

“This volatility is where the real damage happens,” says Wood. “Whether it’s thermal spikes, phase imbalances, or circuit breaker trips – when the power delivery can’t keep up, your own infrastructure becomes the bottleneck.”

This reality is driving a fundamental shift in power infrastructure. Rather than sizing systems to meet peak demand, operators increasingly need to manage power dynamically as workloads change.

## From monitoring to real-time intelligence

The problem with responding to these events effectively is that they can happen faster than traditional monitoring systems can detect them.

Conventional power distribution units (PDUs) typically rely on polling, where readings are requested at intervals of a second or more. This can provide a useful overview of consumption, but it risks missing the more transient events that matter most.

“If you’re polling every second or every few seconds, and you have a millisecond-scale swing, that reading is a snapshot of something that’s already over,” says Wood.

nVent’s approach is based on subsecond sampling and live streaming of power data. Beyond providing a record of what’s happened, the system is designed to provide visibility into how the workload is behaving as it happens.

“You can’t automate what you can’t see in real time,” adds Wood.

## The engine turning data into action

This is where nVent’s Intelligent PDU Platform with built-in event engine secures its place. Traditional metering can deliver accurate information about power consumption and quality, including billing-grade measurements, but this insight is still retrospective. The event engine is designed to take this information and put it into action to trigger an immediate response.

“The event engine can act on what’s happening right now because it runs on the PDU itself,” explains Wood.

The principle is relatively straightforward. An operator establishes a trigger, defines the condition under which it should be sustained, and then specifies the action that follows.

For example, a phase imbalance could be allowed to persist for a defined period before it exceeds a specified threshold and triggers an automated response. This helps prevent the system from reacting to momentary noise while ensuring it responds when it really matters.

## Beyond the PDU

For nVent, the longer-term opportunity lies in connecting power intelligence with the wider data center environment. Once the rack can understand its own power behavior and respond accordingly, this intelligence can be linked with other infrastructure systems, including critical cooling and workload management. This creates the possibility of coordinating systems around what the workload actually needs.

“We’re looking at it from the ground up at the rack level, to help secure better coordination across the entire facility,” says Wood.

nVent’s position is strengthened by its presence across both power and cooling. Rather than treating the two as entirely separate systems, the company is exploring how they can work together to anticipate workload requirements and respond accordingly.

On a broader level, rack-level intelligence can also feed into building management systems and data center infrastructure management software. What starts out as a local response can become part of a wider optimization strategy across the data hall.

This can help deliver more usable capacity from the same footprint, fewer nuisance trips, and closer coordination between power, cooling, and compute.

## The shift towards self-healing infrastructure

The ability to respond automatically is central to another concept Wood highlights: self-healing infrastructure. The term describes a move away from systems that simply identify a problem and notify an operator, towards more proactive infrastructure.

“Most of the infrastructure components and solutions that we use today, especially in power, tell you something went wrong,” says Wood. “What self-healing means is that the power distribution itself can do something about it before you even see the alert.”

Environmental monitoring provides another example. If sensors detect a temperature increase within a cabinet, predefined thresholds could trigger a response such as shutting down non-critical loads, reducing the heat being generated, and giving cooling systems time to react.

Inside high-density environments containing huge volumes of high-value equipment, the stakes are elevated. Consequently, for operators, the appeal of self-healing infrastructure is intrinsically tied to protecting valuable physical and computational investments.

## The bottom line

As rack densities continue to rise, however, intelligent power management will also need to evolve alongside the underlying architecture.

Wood points towards a future in which higher-voltage DC power is delivered directly at the rack, with architectures moving towards 400V and potentially 800V.

By reducing the number of power conversion stages between the source and the compute hardware, operators can potentially reduce losses while freeing up physical space to dedicate to compute.

“It’s a real architectural shift, and it doesn’t happen overnight,” says Wood. “But it’s coming, and rack intelligence has to move with it.”

Ultimately, the argument for intelligent power comes down to the fundamental reality that secured capacity is only valuable if it can actually be deployed effectively.

“The risk has never really been about running out of power. It’s about stranding the power you already have and not making use of it because the rack can’t act fast enough,” he continues.

This makes the rack an increasingly important part of data center power strategies. With real-time visibility, automated responses, and close integration between cooling and workload management, power distribution can become an active participant in infrastructure optimization.

For Wood, the ultimate goal is to ensure that the enormous investments being made in AI infrastructure deliver as much useful compute as possible.

“We invest a lot of money in our data centers today, and it’s really important to be able to make the most of it,” he concludes. “nVent is here to help extract the greatest value out of that investment and to be responsible in our environmental approaches by utilizing our resources most efficiently.”

stories.title: Kinergy bags RM47.5m electrical works contract for hyperscale data centre
stories.summary: Kinergy Advancement has secured a RM47.5 million subcontract from a Gamuda unit to carry out electrical works at a hyperscale data center in Bandar Spring Hill, Port Dickson. The project adds to a cluster of large-scale facilities rising in Negeri Sembilan as developers look beyond the saturated Klang Valley and Johor corridors.
stories.why_it_matters: The subcontract shows Malaysia's data center construction wave cascading down to second-tier electrical contractors and into new geographies like Port Dickson. For the supply chain it means sustained work pipelines; for the market it confirms hyperscale development is diffusing beyond the two established hubs, easing land and power concentration risk.

stories.title_zh: Kinergy赢得4750万令吉合同，为波德申一座hyperscale数据中心提供电气工程服务
stories.summary_zh: Kinergy Advancement 从 Gamuda 旗下子公司获得一份价值 4750 万林吉特的分包合同，负责位于波德申 Bandar Spring Hill 一座 hyperscale data center 的电气工程。随着开发商将目光投向饱和的巴生谷和柔佛走廊之外，森美兰州正崛起一批大型设施集群。
stories.why_zh: 这份分包合同显示，马来西亚的 data center 建设浪潮正传导至二线电气承包商，并向波德申等新区域扩散。对供应链而言，这意味着持续的工程订单；对市场而言，则证实 hyperscale 开发正从两大成熟枢纽向外扩散，有助于缓解土地和电力的集中度风险。
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 12): Kinergy Advancement Bhd (KL:KINERGY) has secured a RM47.5 million subcontract from Gamuda Bhd's (KL:GAMUDA) unit for electrical works at a hyperscale data centre in Bandar Spring Hill, Port Dickson.

The subcontract was awarded by Gamuda Bhd’s wholly-owned subsidiary, Gamuda Engineering Sdn Bhd, for the data centre for a multi-national technology company headquartered in the US. The company was not named in the filing on Monday (Oct 12).

Under the contract, Kinergy will design, supply, install, test and commission the electrical infrastructure, including substations, transformers, power distribution systems, cabling, lighting, backup power systems and EV charging facilities.

The works are scheduled for completion in the first quarter of 2028.

Kinergy’s executive deputy chairman and group managing director Datuk Dr Lai Keng Onn said the award signals the group’s growing recognition in the data centre sector and its technical capabilities in high-specification infrastructure.

Lai cited Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida) figures that showed RM95.8 billion worth of data centre and cloud-computing investments being approved in Malaysia in the first half of 2026.

“As development grows in scale and complexity, we see increasing demand for specialised engineering and power infrastructure, creating a strong opportunity for Kinergy to deepen its participation in the sector,” Lad added.

Kinergy’s share price was unchanged at 39.5 sen during Monday’s mid-day break, valuing it at RM852.31 million.

stories.title: Bain's Bridge Data Centres seeks to upsize loan to US$6.6 billion
stories.summary: Bridge Data Centres, the Bain Capital-owned pan-Asian platform, is seeking to upsize an existing loan facility to US$6.6 billion. If completed, the financing would rank among the largest debt deals ever struck in Asia's data center sector, reflecting the scale of capital required for hyperscale expansion across the region.
stories.why_it_matters: A loan of this size signals that lenders still view Asian hyperscale data centers as bankable at scale, even as equity markets grow cautious. It also raises the leverage bar for competitors: operators without access to comparable debt capacity risk falling behind in land and power acquisition races across key APAC markets.

stories.title_zh: 贝恩资本旗下Bridge Data Centres寻求将贷款规模扩大至66亿美元
stories.summary_zh: 贝恩资本（Bain Capital）旗下的泛亚平台 Bridge Data Centres 正寻求将现有贷款规模扩大至 66 亿美元。若最终完成，该融资将成为亚洲 data center 行业有史以来最大规模的债务交易之一，反映出该区域 hyperscale 扩张所需的庞大资本量。
stories.why_zh: 如此大规模的贷款表明，即便股票市场趋于谨慎，贷款机构仍认为亚洲 hyperscale data center 在大规模层面具备可融资性。这也抬高了竞争对手的杠杆门槛：无法获得同等债务融资能力的运营商，可能在亚太主要市场的土地和电力资源争夺战中掉队。
stories.content:
This will be one of the largest deals for the sector in Asia

\[HONG KONG\] Bain Capital-owned Bridge Data Centres is in talks with banks to more than double the size of an existing loan to about US$6.6 billion, people familiar with the matter said, in what would be one of the largest deals for the sector in Asia.

The move is an extension of a previous effort to increase the size to at least US$5 billion from an original US$2.8 billion that it obtained last year for its operations in Malaysia.

The expanded deal could be launched into the market as early as November, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussion private matters.

At the same time, plans for a loan of up to US$6 billion for a Thailand-based data centre have stalled, the people said, around the time the South-east Asian nation decided last month to suspend the construction of 49 data centres amid concerns over energy usage.

A spokesperson for Bridge said “as a matter of policy, we do not comment on unverified information or market speculation”.

Data centre operators have been rushing to take on additional debt as they seek to expand amid growing demand spurred by the AI boom. Moody’s Ratings expects at least US$3 trillion to flow into data centre-related investments over the next five years, with much of the spending financed through debt.

Still, signs are emerging that global investors are starting to push back when they perceive valuations to be frothy. Banks are increasingly mindful of their exposure to the sector as they bump-up against lending limits.

The most salient recent example of investor hesitation came just last week when Firmus Grid pulled an attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever initial public offerings after running into difficulties convincing some potential investors of its steep increase in market value.

Wall Street has grown increasingly anxious about AI and its potential to impact other businesses, a fear that spurred investors to dump a range of stocks from Expedia to Salesforce earlier this year.

BDC is a unit of Wintrix, formerly known as Chindata Group, the Chinese data centre operator that Bain Capital took private in 2023 in a deal worth about US$3.2 billion. The firm currently has facilities in Malaysia, Thailand, and India, according to its company website. BLOOMBERG

# SM+ acquires Princeton Digital Group's Indonesian enterprise data centers

PT SMPlus Digital Investama (SM+) has signed an agreement to acquire Princeton Digital Group's (PDG) enterprise data center business in Indonesia. The acquisition includes five operational facilities across key Indonesian markets.

- Published On Oct 12, 2026 at 09:35 AM IST

## Highlights

- SM+ acquires five operational enterprise data centers from Princeton Digital Group in Indonesia.
- The acquisition expands SM+'s digital infrastructure footprint to 31 sites across 25 Indonesian cities.
- Princeton Digital Group will now focus on its hyperscale data center portfolio in Indonesia.
- The acquired facilities are located in Greater Jakarta, Bandung, Surabaya, and Pekanbaru.

## Comments

What are your thoughts?

stories.title: SM+ to Acquire Princeton Digital Group's Enterprise Data Center Business in Indonesia
stories.summary: Indonesian digital infrastructure firm PT SMPlus Digital Investama (SM+) has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Princeton Digital Group's (PDG) enterprise data center business in Indonesia. The deal covers five operational facilities located across the country, expanding SM+'s footprint in one of Southeast Asia's fastest-growing digital infrastructure markets.
stories.why_it_matters: The transaction marks a significant consolidation in Indonesia's data center market, shifting five live facilities from a regional hyperscale player to a domestic operator. For PDG it frees capital for larger hyperscale builds elsewhere in Asia, while enterprise and cloud customers in Indonesia will watch whether service terms and expansion plans change under new ownership.
stories.title_zh: SM+ 将收购 Princeton Digital Group 在印尼的企业数据中心业务
stories.summary_zh: 印尼数字基础设施公司 PT SMPlus Digital Investama（SM+）已签署最终协议，收购 Princeton Digital Group（PDG）在印尼的 enterprise data center 业务。此次交易涵盖位于印尼各地的五座已投入运营的设施，扩大了 SM+ 在东南亚增长最快的数字基础设施市场之一的布局。
stories.why_zh: 这笔交易标志着印尼 data center 市场的一次重要整合，五座在运设施从区域性 hyperscale 运营商转手至本土运营商。对 PDG 而言，这释放了资金用于亚洲其他地区更大规模的 hyperscale 建设；而印尼的企业和云客户将关注新东家是否会改变服务条款与扩张计划。
stories.content:
Indonesian digital infrastructure firm PT SMPlus Digital Investama (together with its affiliates, “SM+”), announced today that it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire the enterprise data centre business in Indonesia held by Princeton Digital Group (PDG), according to statements by the firms.

The business acquired includes five high-quality, operational data centre facilities located across key Indonesian markets, namely Greater Jakarta, Bandung, Surabaya and Pekanbaru.

This acquisition will help strengthen and expand SM+ digital infrastructure platform in Indonesia, which is experiencing strong growth in data consumption, cloud adoption and enterprise digital transformation. The firm further expects to enhance service delivery, support future growth opportunities and continue enabling Indonesia’s digital transformation through this transaction.

With this deal, SM+ will be operating 31 sites in 25 cities or markets in Indonesia.

“This acquisition marks an important milestone in our journey to build Indonesia’s leading home-grown digital infrastructure platform. By adding five facilities across Greater Jakarta, Bandung, Surabaya and Pekanbaru, we are expanding our nationwide footprint and strengthening our ability to serve customers as we continue supporting Indonesia’s digital economy,” said Herson Suindah, President Director and Group CEO of SM+ Holdings.

 “Indonesia is a key market for PDG since entering the market in 2019. We acquired these enterprise-grade sites as part of our ‘enter-and-expand’ strategy of market entry and have since developed a hyperscale data center portfolio of \~400 MW in the country. Our focus will continue to be to build on that hyperscale portfolio (which includes the JC2, JC3 and JC4 campuses, with further expansion underway) and to enhance our leadership position in Indonesia,” said Varoon Raghavan, Chief Operating Officer and Co-Founder of Princeton Digital Group.

PDG’s total portfolio exceeds 1.8 GW across eight countries in Asia Pacific.

The transaction remains subject to customary closing conditions. UBS AG Singapore Branch is acting as exclusive financial advisor to SM+ on the transaction.

stories.title: DayOne in Talks for US$500 Million Bond: Report
stories.summary: Singapore-headquartered DayOne Data Centers has been in discussions with banks for several weeks about a potential US$500 million bond offering that could launch as early as next year, according to Bloomberg. The Citigroup-arranged deal would fund the company's project pipeline as the GDS-spun-off platform expands across Asia-Pacific.
stories.why_it_matters: A successful bond sale would give DayOne independent access to capital markets separate from its GDS heritage, testing investor appetite for Southeast Asian data center credit. The timing and pricing will serve as a benchmark for other regional platforms weighing bond financing against private debt.

stories.summary_zh: 据彭博社报道，总部位于新加坡的 DayOne Data Centers 已与多家银行就潜在 5 亿美元债券发行讨论数周，最早可能于明年推向市场。该笔由花旗集团（Citigroup）安排的债券将用于资助公司项目管线，支持这家从 GDS 分拆出来的平台在亚太地区扩张。

stories.content:
Singapore-based data center platform DayOne Data Centers Ltd has been discussing with banks for weeks about a potential US$500 million bond offering which could go to the market as early as next year, Bloomberg reports quoting people familiar with the matter.

The people added the bond offerring which is arranged by Citigroup Inc is to finance projects but did not specify which particular projects. If successful, this would be one of the first data center bond offerrings in Asia Pacific.

This is despite one of its project partners, Nvidia Corp-backed Firmus Grid Ltd, abandoning an initial public offering in Australia last week. This would have been one of Australia’s largest IPOs and the proceeds would have funded purchases of graphics processing units (GPUs) for its planned first data center project in Batam, Indonesia, as part of an eight-year partnership with Nvidia. DayOne would have been the co-developer of the data center.

Last week, DayOne had filed for a US IPO for a potential US$5 billion raise as the firm ramps up fundraising to meet insatiable demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

DayOne had earlier closed half of a US$7 billion-equivalent loan supported by more than 30 lenders. The firm is also seeking a HK$1.86 billion (US$237 million) loan for a Hong Kong data center. In August, DayOne secured a four-year S$530 million (US$414 million) to develop its first data center in Singapore.

DayOne features footprint in Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Japan, Hong Kong, Thailand and Finland.

Representatives for DayOne and Citigroup declined to comment when requested.

stories.title: Architecting digital trust for Malaysia's sovereign AI future
stories.summary: Artificial intelligence is moving into the systems that power banking, public services, industry and critical infrastructure. But having the computing power to run AI is only part of the story. Malaysia also needs to secure its data, test how AI systems perform and know whether their outputs can be trusted.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: 为马来西亚主权AI未来构建数字信任架构
stories.content:
Artificial intelligence is moving into the systems that power banking, public services, industry and critical infrastructure. But having the computing power to run AI is only part of the story. Malaysia also needs to secure its data, test how AI systems perform and know whether their outputs can be trusted.

This is the role MIMOS Berhad is looking to play as Malaysia builds its own sovereign AI capabilities, with Group Chief Technology Officer Dr Zulaikha Kadim working across areas including deepfake detection, AI-driven cybersecurity, trusted digital identity and cognitive AI.

As AI takes on bigger, higher-stakes roles, it can no longer be judged simply by how fast or intelligent it is, she says. Its outputs must also be accurate, secure, explainable and accountable.

“AI is no longer used only to generate text or images. It is increasingly being embedded into systems that influence decisions in public services, industry, finance and critical infrastructure,” she points out.

In other words, AI now has to be checked and proven, not just made faster or smarter. That is the idea behind Digital Trust: being able to rely on what a digital system tells you, whether a transaction is genuine, a person is who they claim to be, or a record has not been changed.

MIMOS is developing these digital trust capabilities through its Trusted Intelligence Platform, as part of its efforts to turn national priorities into technologies that can be tested locally. The two concepts are closely linked, but Zulaikha says they serve different purposes.

“Digital Trust is the confidence that people and organisations have in a digital system, transaction or AI-supported decision. They need to know that the system is secure, that the information has not been altered and that the identity or content involved is genuine,” she explains.

That work is aligned with Malaysia’s broader push to build trusted and sovereign AI capabilities, with MIMOS translating national priorities into technologies that can be developed and tested locally.

Under the 13th Malaysia Plan (RMK13), MIMOS is developing blockchain-secured trusted logs, deepfake detection and AI-driven cybersecurity, as well as Mi-Muallim, which detects deviations in verified content. The work also extends to cognitive AI for vision and robotics.

Deepfakes are one area where the technology is being put to the test. MIMOS is developing detection tools while studying how synthetic and manipulated content is created, allowing researchers to understand how quickly the technology behind such manipulation is evolving.

“MIMOS is addressing deepfakes from both the defensive and research perspectives. Under RMK13, we are developing AI-based detection technologies to assess multimedia integrity, while researching generative AI to understand how synthetic and manipulated content is created,” says Zulaikha.

But detection alone is not enough. She says the technology also has to work in Malaysia, where language, accents and demographics can differ from the data used to train overseas models.

“Localisation is equally important. Detection models developed overseas may not perform consistently with Bahasa Melayu, mixed-language conversations, Malaysian accents or our diverse population,” she adds.

This means building local datasets and testing methods to give organisations evidence they can use in investigations, risk assessments and operational decisions. From there, MIMOS takes the technology into controlled proof-of-concept projects with users, testing how it performs in real operating environments before wider deployment.

“Their feedback also allows us to refine the technology around genuine requirements rather than assumptions made by researchers. Therefore, the objective is not to conduct a showcase for its own sake. It is to generate evidence, confirm the value proposition and create a credible pathway towards adoption and commercialisation,” says Zulaikha.

That approach also shapes how MIMOS works alongside global technology providers as Malaysia expands its cloud, data centre and computing capacity. Sovereignty does not mean shutting out global technology, but retaining control over sensitive data and critical AI capabilities, she says.

“Global technology providers give Malaysia access to advanced cloud infrastructure, computing platforms, foundational AI models and global innovation networks. We should benefit from their speed, scale and investment. However, Malaysia must retain the ability to protect sensitive data, verify how an AI system performs in our environment and decide which workloads should remain local or on-premises,” she adds.

MIMOS therefore takes a hybrid approach to computing, combining its own on-premises graphics processing units with secure cloud resources and infrastructure from strategic partners. Sensitive workloads can remain in controlled local environments, while larger workloads can use external infrastructure where appropriate.

“The important point is that sovereignty is not determined only by who owns the hardware. It also depends on whether Malaysia retains control over its data, models, security requirements and critical AI capabilities,” she says.

The longer-term opportunity is to turn those capabilities into platforms, standards and assurance services that can be deployed beyond individual projects.

“If we can convert these capabilities into repeatable platforms, standards and assurance services, Malaysia can support both domestic adoption and regional deployment. The opportunity is larger than becoming a user or host of AI infrastructure,” says Zulaikha.

“Malaysia can become a regional location where high-impact AI and digital content are independently tested, validated and trusted. That is where technological sovereignty can translate into economic value.”

For more on MIMOS’ applied research and development work, visit mimos.my.

stories.title: Nvidia weighs deeper ties with open-model developer Reflection AI through investment or computing deal
stories.summary: Reflection has also struck billion-dollar deals with SpaceX and cloud provider Nebius Group
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia backing an open-model developer would blur the line between chip supplier and ecosystem kingmaker, giving it influence over the software stack that competes with closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic — both also dependent on Nvidia hardware. For data center operators, alignment between GPU supply and open-model adoption could steer demand patterns, while Reflection's deals with SpaceX and Nebius show open models are now commanding hyperscale-level capital commitments.
stories.title_zh: NVIDIA考虑通过投资或算力交易加深与开源模型开发商Reflection AI的合作
stories.content:
Reflection has also struck billion-dollar deals with SpaceX and cloud provider Nebius Group

NVIDIA is in talks to boost its investment in Reflection AI or offer the US startup computing power, a move that would strengthen ties with a key developer of open-weight models, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The discussions are at an early stage, and no terms have been reached, said the person, who asked not to be identified because the matter is private. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment, while Reflection declined to comment.

The *Financial Times* previously reported on the talks, saying they could potentially lead to an acquisition offer. Possible deal structures include an “acqui-hire,” in which Nvidia would hire staff and license technology; an agreement to provide the startup with more chips; or an increase in Nvidia’s equity investment, the newspaper said.

The startup debuted its first open-weight model, Beam, earlier in October, pushing into a market where Chinese startups have a strong presence. With such software, developers release the model’s parameters, or weights, allowing others to freely use and modify the technology.

Beam is designed to perform well for business customers and developers on coding and AI agent tasks while costing less than many competitors’ products, Reflection said on Monday (Oct 5). It said Beam scores comparably on advanced reasoning benchmarks to GLM-5.2, a flagship open model from China’s Z.AI.

The startup, which was founded by two former Google DeepMind researchers, has held talks to raise US$2.5 billion at a valuation of US$25 billion, the *Wall Street Journal* previously reported.

Reflection has also struck billion-dollar deals with Elon Musk’s SpaceX and cloud provider Nebius Group to secure computing power to develop its models.

A Reflection tie-up would add to a frenzy of transactions by Nvidia in recent months. The chipmaker, which is the world’s most valuable company, has used its financial might to cultivate the broader AI industry.

The deals have included a US$13 billion agreement to buy AI model company Hugging Face in September and a roughly US$20 billion licensing pact with the chip startup Groq.

Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang is also a major proponent of open-weight models.

The hope is that US development of the technology could curb startups’ use of Chinese open-weight models, which are much cheaper to use than ones from American companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, while not far behind in intelligence.

The US government is also encouraging the development of such models.

“We need to ensure America has leading open models founded on American values,” reads US President Donald Trump’s July 2025 AI action plan. “Open-source and open-weight models could become global standards in some areas of business and in academic research worldwide.” BLOOMBERG
